stem:
Girish plans to spot Venus from the roof of his flat in Pune at 7:30 p.m. on a Tuesday in March. Venus is above the horizon then, but a thick layer of monsoon-like cloud covers the whole sky and nearby street lamps stay on.

Which judgment about seeing Venus that evening is correct?

options.text: He will see Venus clearly because it is above the horizon at that clock time.
He is unlikely to see Venus because clouds and bright city lights block a clear dark view, even though the planet is above the horizon.
Switching on more roof lights will make Venus easier to find against the clouds.
Venus can be seen from every place on Earth at 7:30 p.m. that Tuesday, so cloud cover does not matter.

teacher.key_rationale: Visibility needs the object above the horizon plus clear, sufficiently dark sky. Clouds and light pollution can hide Venus even when the time is right.
